sentences.text: A complete skeleton discovered in 1995 shows that the species M. planirostris reached a length of about 4 meters.
This species possesses a plain snout that lacks any bony ornamentation or crests.
Scientists propose that soft tissue structures, perhaps keratinous crests, may have covered the snout of M. planirostris.
In contrast, the other species, M. westphali, displays multiple bony crests along the upper jaw, particularly at the snout's base and tip.
The tail accounts for 51% of the total body length, exceeding the combined length of all other body parts.
Its elongated jaws resemble those of modern gharials, suggesting a diet focused primarily on fish.
Analysis of tooth microwear indicates the animal also consumed softer invertebrates alongside fish.
The tail features an inverted 'T' shape of chevrons, a trait unique to Mystriosuchus among phytosaurs but found in sauropterygians and some crocodilians.
The genus authority is attributed to Eberhard Fraas in 1896.
Two species are recognized within the genus: M. westphali and the type species M. planirostris.
Later cladistic analysis grouped Mystriosuchus with Pseudopalatinae rather than its former subfamily, Mystriosuchidae.
Christian Kammerer and colleagues synonymized Pseudopalatinae with Mystriosuchini because the latter name holds priority.
Consequently, Mystriosuchus belongs to the parent group Mystriosuchini.
Fossils of this creature have been recovered from Europe and Greenland during the Late Triassic, specifically the middle Norian stage.
The temporal range extends from the Norian to the Hettangian, spanning between 227.3 and 199.5 million years ago.
While originally considered a freshwater dweller, some specimens from Northern Italy suggest a completely marine lifestyle.
